title: Story-Based Decision Making: The Better Story Method
opening: An option can sound exciting before you have checked what it would involve. Compare what you would actually do, what it would cost and the commitments you would need to keep. Then ask which experience would be more meaningful to live and remember.

labels.comparisonIntro: Imagine you could take an exciting trip to investigate an idea with a collaborator, or stay home to keep a worthy commitment you already made. The trip is not automatically better because it sounds exciting. Compare the real timing, cost, people affected, and what each ordinary day would involve before asking which experience matters more to you.
labels.tripText: Possible ordinary days: travel, investigate the idea, and make time for the collaborator. Check the actual cost, dates, preparation, and any people depending on you.
labels.commitmentText: Possible ordinary days: stay, do the work you promised, and let the collaborator know what you can realistically offer later. Check what the commitment is, who relies on it, and whether another arrangement is possible.
labels.decisionTitle: Use the story after the facts
labels.decisionText: When both routes are feasible, ask which experience you would find more meaningful to live and remember, and why. Excitement is one clue about what matters; it does not settle feasibility or consequences. If a clear obligation determines the choice, honor it without forcing a dramatic story exercise.
labels.practiceIntro: Write what each choice would ask of an ordinary day, including its costs and commitments. Your notes are optional and private. You can save a partial note and return later.
labels.private: This optional private note stays separate from the six required course questions.

labels.sourceQuote:
Story-Based Decision Making: The Better Story Method
Adapted from Amjad Masad’s Better Story approach, this asks which experience you
want to live. At a crossroads, compare the actual paths first. Then ask which
experience you would find more meaningful to live and remember. Record why the
answer matters and what choosing it involves. Use a brief daily story prompt when
the same question helps a smaller decision.

fields.label: Route A: what would the actual path and ordinary days involve?
Route B: what would the actual path and ordinary days involve?
What costs, preparation, and commitments come with each route?
If both routes are feasible, which experience would be more meaningful to live and remember, and why?
What fact, clear obligation, or next decision should guide what happens?

example.crossroads: Hypothetical only: I could take an exciting trip to investigate an idea with a collaborator, or stay to keep a worthy commitment I already made.
example.routeA: The trip means travel, shared investigation, and time with the collaborator. I would need to confirm dates, cost, preparation, and who else depends on me.
example.routeB: Staying means doing the work I promised and telling the collaborator what I could realistically offer later. I would check whether the commitment is still due and whether any alternative is fair to the people involved.
example.costsCommitments: The trip costs money and time and may affect people relying on my promise. Staying may delay the investigation and also has a real opportunity cost. I would check the actual terms before choosing.
example.meaning: If the commitment can be kept another way and both options are feasible, I would compare the ordinary days and choose the experience I most want to live and remember. The trip sounding exciting by itself would not decide it.
example.nextFact: First confirm the dates and what the commitment requires. If it is a clear obligation, keep it and discuss a later investigation with the collaborator.
